Content:
32:00

What idealistic nonsense. This is yet another repetition of the American fairy tale that “everything starts with one person who simply believes in themselves.” No — the world doesn’t change because a stubborn dreamer with an idea appears. That’s just a comforting narrative for those who live inside the American ideology of individualism. Reality works very differently.

One person without a material base cannot start any “movement,” no matter how determined they are. For an idea to even reach “10 people,” it requires resources: time, money, connections, infrastructure. The world changes only when someone with access to capital and material capabilities enters the picture. Because that “stubborn visionary with capital” doesn’t have to spend their life fighting for basic survival.

It’s easy to preach about “believing in yourself” and “the power of the individual” while sitting in the U.S., with a financial safety net, family support, social mobility, and the privileges of belonging to a global elite that extracts rent from the rest of the world. But for those exploited by this very “golden billion,” this rhetoric isn’t inspiring — it’s insulting. People outside your privileged bubble cannot “just start,” because they lack even the minimum conditions to survive, let alone “change the world.”

History also does not support this romantic narrative. The world was not changed by random lone geniuses “with an idea in their head,” but by elites or those closely tied to them — people with resources, patrons, education, and power. Even ideas born “from below” only became influential once they were adopted, financed, and amplified by those with resources. And conversely — harmful or disastrous ideas reshaped the world too, when backed by capital and the machinery of power.

This American slogan, “it all starts with you, just believe,” is a convenient lie for the wealthy world. It erases global inequality and shifts responsibility onto those whom the system deprives of resources in the first place.

No — this idealistic rhetoric only works for the oversaturated and globally privileged citizens of the Western world, who already begin life from a position of enormous advantage. For ordinary people kept at the bottom of the system, this narrative is not just false — it’s offensive.

Author: @GeneralJug
Content: I wonder what would happen if you weighed different connections differently. Like, acquaintances would be a 10% connection, close friends would be a 90% connection. Then you multiply the percents together for chains. So if I have a 90% connection to one friend, who has a 90% connection to another, who has a 90% connection to, say, Vsauce, I'd have a 72.9% connection to Vsauce (because 0.9^3=0.729). But I also might have a 10% connection to somebody else, and that somebody else has their own 10% connection to Vsauce. This new chain makes me 1% connected to Vsauce. It's a shorter chain because there are less middlemen, but it's a "weaker" chain because the people within the chain are less connected to each other. It sort of goes against the whole small world idea, not valuing the weaker connections as much, but I still am interested to see what properties this type of world would have!

Author: @DavZell
Content: 2 minutes in, and I feel you've made a serious math assumption error.   Your math assumes that each the members in each group of 100 doesn't overlap in who they know.  Of your 100, how many come from groups that result in overlap when moving to their 100?  Work, school, hobbies, family, religion - each group canceling out part of the next 100.  If your 100 came from 10 groups, and the people in each group know each other, the exponentiation falls apart, as you are overcounting each set of subsequent connections exponentially.  The collapse gets worse when you consider other connections between your groups.  Its like a complex set of Venn diagrams.

Content:
Yep. I know someone from Britain, someone from Scotland, someone from Canada, someone from Australia, and someone from Mexico. I know people from all different walks of life. I know people who have government jobs, people who make art, a guy who's a boxer, people in tech, people in scientific research, and the list goes on. It's fascinating how we're all connected. It's interesting that everyone who knows me could get to know the people I know if they wanted to.
The solution to all of this is nuanced thinking, impulse control, and empathy. Ignore people who bring you negativity if you can and they aren't willing to change. Be kind to people you have to interact with, even if they're rude to you, and assume there's a good reason for their behavior. Someone was rude to you? Maybe they were having a tough day and just hit their breaking point. Someone is speeding? Maybe they needed to get to the hospital. Someone shuts down your ideas? Maybe they weren't taught how to work with other people. This works because it keeps you positive and doesn't feed other people's negativity. Yes, sometimes your optimism will be wrong, but is that really going to effect things? No, you get the same result. If something is really an issue, address the concern in a productive way or let it go. Don't harbor that bad energy.

Author: @glennsampson5945
Content:
The "six degrees of separation" is a misstatement of an experiment.  A mathematical model determined that the given any two people, there was a 99% chance that they could be connected through 2 intermediaries.  To test this out, they picked pairs of random people who did not know each other and were in vastly different locations.  They gave one person an object with the following instructions.  If you know the other person, send it to them.  Otherwise send it to the person you think is most likely to know them and pass along the instructions.  On average, it took six steps to reach the other person.

The claim that you can reach every person by only six steps is decidedly false.  To demonstrate this, all you have to do is take one person who lives in an isolated tribe and another person who is not a member of this tribe.  For example, the people of North Sentinel Island (in the northern Indian Ocean) have lived in isolation from the rest of humanity for 60,000 years.  If one person is a member of these people and another is not, you will not be able to link them in any number of steps.

Note: The government of India has declared the Island off limits.  This is both for the protection of any attempted visitors -- those very few that have attempted to contact them were immediately killed, and for the protection of the indigenous population -- introducing a disease for which they have no protection could wipe out the entire population.

Author: @SivadBop
Content:
I loved the video and the message, but am I the only one that felt something politically suggestive, and potentially a dark side to the human reaction to this phenomenon?

What I mean is we are kinda seeing a reaction, globally, to the negative "shortcut" effects of the internet and social networking at the scale of civic society. And while one approach to that problem is "be nicer," another could be "make your network smaller." In the language of networking, that means severing the shortcuts and far-flung connections, determining and enforcing who is in-group and out-group, etc. 

It's pretty obvious to see how this urge toward in-control networks also can become nativism, paranoia, antipathy toward foreigners, and on and on. We hear, especially in the USA, a lot these days about who are friends/enemies, who belongs/doesn't, and about the virtues of "traditional" networks, especially the types that existed pre-internet.

I'm not even taking sides here. I sympathize, or understand on some level, the desire to exist in a managable network in which you retain some identity and agency. I also see how it could pretty readily convince someone that we need to shut off all immigration and insist fervently on all foreigners integrating fully to our own arbitrary set of cultural standards. There is not a simple, sunny takeaway from this video and it opens lot of uneasy and pertinent questions.

Author: @fastnoc
Content:
This topic hits close to home. Back in the late ’90s, a business partner and I built something remarkably similar while experimenting with early web analytics and referral tracking.

At the time, Google’s algorithm heavily rewarded backlinks.  The more sites linking to you, the higher you rank. Bloggers were constantly trading links manually, messaging each other to “swap favors.” I wondered: what if we automated that entire process?

We developed a snippet of code that bloggers could paste into their pages. It automatically tracked where visitors came from and displayed a live, hyperlinked list of referring sites. In seconds, a site could show exactly who was linking to them.  No outreach, no negotiation, just real-time reciprocity.

We launched it quietly as a proof-of-concept, free to use. Within weeks, it exploded. By the early 2000s, we were tracking billions of hits a day across an equally staggering number of sites. It became a kind of underground standard for link exchange in the blogosphere.

The data we collected was mind-blowing.  A real-world visualization of the “six degrees of separation” concept. You could see digital communities forming before social media existed: politics, hobbies, tech, art. All clustering naturally through mutual links.

Unfortunately, our main business took priority, and we eventually shelved the project instead of scaling or selling it. A missed opportunity, maybe, but it led us toward something even bigger — we went on to create one of the first rentable multiplayer game server networks, using Quake II’s dedicated server code. That one changed everything.

In hindsight, it’s fascinating to see how ideas born out of curiosity in that era ended up predicting where the internet and human connection was headed.

Love this channel. Incredible research, and it’s great to see topics like this explored with such depth.

The travels we have to other places are the shortcuts you talk about. I think it’s fair to say that there are certain people in certain industries that act as hubs too. It would take two steps just to get from a young member to an elder to someone who has met outsiders - an anthropologist. So now if we map out that anthropologist's six degrees of separation, we can confidently say that everyone who is 5 or 6 steps removed, is 7 or 8 steps removed from that young member of the tribal community.

Author: @antecbox
Content: This video clearly illustrates the failure of the modern multicultural experiment. Societies aren’t held together by slogans about “diversity is a strength,” but by organic networks with the hubs and nodes of shared values, culture, and history. When those foundational bonds are eroded, social cohesion collapses, leaving behind a disconnected mass with no shared identity. As this research above shows, the consequences are inevitably negative. The elites and media may keep insisting that this imposed fragmentation equals strength, but the lived reality in every major city tells a different story. Breaking legacy hubs doesn’t create integration, it breeds erosion of cohesion and institutional decay, while select groups gain special rights and privileges, strengthening their own networks at the expense of everyone else, compounding and increasing division and instability. The data and lived experience both point to the same truth that cohesion cannot be manufactured through forced diversity. True unity is not imposed, it’s cultivated through shared heritage and mutual trust. Ultimately civilization depends not on how many cultures it collects, but on how well it preserves the foundations that made it whole. Let's hope we can change this before its too late.

Author: @sherryrizz
Content:
A few days ago, a friend from another town called me. He was searching online for a second-hand bike and found someone willing to sell one. The seller lived in a town that was much closer to me than to him, so he asked if I could go check the bike to see if it was in good condition.
Now, while the town was indeed nearer to me than to my friend, it still wasn’t close enough for me to just casually head over. Plus, I don’t exactly trust my own judgment when it comes to bikes. So my brain immediately started looking for a workaround.
That’s when I remembered another friend who happened to be friends with a bike mechanic in the same town where the seller lived. I called him up and asked for the mechanic’s number. At the same time, I asked the friend who wanted to buy the bike to send me the seller’s number.
My plan was simple. I’d ask the seller to take the bike to the mechanic, who could then check its condition and let me know. I’d pass that info along to my friend, and he could decide whether to go ahead with the purchase.
But then came the twist. When both friends sent me the numbers, they turned out to be the same. The seller and the mechanic were the same person.
So yeah, turns out my grand plan to involve a third party ended up being a one-man show. The seller was the mechanic. The mechanic was the seller. I had unknowingly planned the perfect inspection by asking the seller to inspect his own bike.

Author: @hardlyb
Content: This property shows up in all sorts of data, not just personal connections. For lots of types of data, if you define a natural metric - that is, a distance function which experts on that data regard as reasonable - you find that taking a relatively small number of nearest nbrs and using those as your 'links', in most cases you get graphs which look like the ones being described here. Even more interesting, these links turn out to be a much better description of the data than the distance function - the data where the links disagree with the distance function are often quite interesting.

It's basically similar to Kademlia, a distributed hash table (DHT) protocol. It's more or less a P2P method to achieves efficient node lookups with a time complexity of O(log N), where N represents the total number of nodes in the network.

Author: @Harrery
Content:
I think most people assume 8 billion is a large number but they don’t know how exponents work.  

Just squaring something raises it by the power of 2.  So if everyone knew 2 people, then each degree of separation would double or times 2.

But what if each person knows 100 different people.  Muiply that by 100 instead of just doubling (add two 00s to the number each iteration or each degree of separation).

A billion is only nine 0s which is only 4.5 people needing to know 100 different people to reach.

This does make a lot of assumptions like everyone knows exactly 100 unique people and are contacting the exact proper person at the right time in order to reach the targeted goal but it ends up making sense that it’s around 4-5 people on average, 6 degrees would make 1 trillion connections using this formula

Content:
The hub node graph is so interesting to me, bc Tumblr has the option to show engagement with a given post as a graph, where different users are represented by dots and connections (reblogs) are represented by lines and these graphs look exactly like that visualisation.
Also, interestingly enough, in the past (around the 2010s, I think) there was a move in air travel to create hub systems where you have big, central hubs in large cities that were connected to each other and then have smaller regional airports connect to these hubs, rather than to each other. In more recent years the move has actually been away from that bc it's just a lot less fuel efficient (the worst parts of a flight for the environment are take-off and landing) This is also why large planes like the A380 are slowly disappearing again. They only really make sense for a hub network. Once you go away from that, it's more useful to have smaller planes, bc suddenly not as many people are flying from the hubs.

Content:
At around 20:21 it sounds like (and is transcribed by Youtube as) Barabási and Albert, but his name is Albert-László Barabási (one person). He's nationality is hungarian, but he was born in Transylvania, Romania. 
In Romania, giving your child a middle* name is technically not possible, but many Hungarians living there result to hyphenating two existing first names, going around the technicality. So his name is the same as Albert László Barabási would be.
Why did I add an asterisk to "middle name"? Because Hungarians use their family name first, so what is in the middle in most languages, is at the end of the name.
So "Barabási Albert László" is the way his name would be written in Hungary. If you check his Wikipedia page in Hungarian, it is how he is mentioned there.

Author: @EfficientRVer
Content:
Six degrees is child's play if a few of your "shortcuts" turn out to be "hubs".  Among chess players, the equivalent of Bacon number is your Morphy number.  Paul Morphy was the first world champion of chess, in the 1800s.  If you played him, your Morphy number is 1.  If you played someone who played him, 2.  Etc.  I'm 68 and my Morphy number is 5, and in hindsight I had some opportunities to make it 4, before it "was a thing."   While I'm not a great chess player, I was the best in my high school, and can give better players a good game as often as not.  One kid I played while in my teens, later became a Grandmaster, who then played many old Grandmasters, so he was one of my 4 separate paths to Morphy number 5.  Another was a kid I played many games while in high school, who lived two towns away.  At some point, he played a very old master in a tournament, who in retrospect was a 3, making him a 4 and me a 5.  In college, a fellow student was a Grandmaster who left professional chess to get a graduate degree, and I played him one time.   My 4th path to it was a low-level master I played while a teen, who later became an International Master and would gamble against anyone willing to play speed games against him at NYC chess clubs.  One documented opponend was a very famous old guy who was a 3, again making him a 4 and me a 5.

So, 5 degrees of separation to someone who was active for only a short while around  1-2/3 centuries ago!  

I'm 2 to most world champions from Smyslov to Carlson.  But 3 to Bobby Fischer, who was reclusive and didn't play that many people!  Again, I'm not a great or important chess player, at all, but I'm about as connected to chess players as a golfer would be if he had teed it up with Jack Nicklaus, or at least Tom Kite.

The closer you look, the more connections you can find.  I think the reason people may need 6 rather than 4 or 5 to some particular person, is that either they or that person, either don't have many shortcut/hub connections, or just can't find documentation of what the connections between the middle people are.  Rarely is it the famous person who lacks the connections, or people remembering that they are connected to them.  

The strength or weakness of the connection does matter.  I don't generally consider someone an acquaintance/connection if I just met them at a book signing or attended a performance of theirs, etc.  Speaking for several minutes, and the interest in doing so being mutual, is pretty much were I draw the line.  Another way I draw the line is if they recognize and greet me the next time we run across each other.   It helps tell you whether it is a 1-way celeb/fan type thing, or you actually became someone they remember and are glad to see again.  

An interesting correlation I found is that of the various types of celebs I've met, the ones most likely to remember/greet me a year after only speaking briefly, are IndyCar drivers.  Mears, Andretti, and Fittipaldi not only recognized me long after that became a superhuman feat due to the number of people they see, but they sometimes could also rattle off what races they saw me at in the stands, when we had not crossed paths.  As in, saw me from the moving race car, and rememberd it 2 years later.  Their senses, attention to detail, and memory are just at another level.  And I found them to be very warm and personable, for how busy they are.

Rock stars, if we'd spent say 5 minutes talking, they might not remember.  But 15 or 30 minutes and having a mutual friend, they'd remember, but not necessarily warm up to you.

Astronauts, somewhere in between, but the really famous ones seem to not bother even trying to remember most people.  Instead, they seem to decide when with you in an early encounter, whether to consider you an acquaintance, friend, or just another pest looking for their attention, which they politely deal with.  They are either in "putting up with people" mode where you feel connected but they don't, or they warm up to you and they probably value the connection more than you do, because the ratio of pests to people treating them as humans, is pretty dismal.  Once they like you, they'd stop and change your flat tire for you, if they spotted you at the side of the road.

I guess that they realize that pests = what are called defectors in this video.  If you raise that cooperation and kindness paddle every time, even while defectors are walking away with autographs and photos while you are not, they will notice.  In my case, it was never as a strategy, it was just being nice, and a Golden Rule thing.  

Same as why I try to be as nice as I can to every partner.  If I didn't feel like being nice to her, what is the point in wanting to be with her?  If we both keep raising that green cooperation paddle, it's a good sign.  If the red defector paddle comes up too often from a partner, do I even want to play the game of tit for tat to incentivize her to be nice?  Not really.  I'd rather find someone who's naturally nice, rather than someone who's just strategizing to optimize what they can get out of me.

Author: @jkrumins2723
Content:
Wow, 10,000 comments already, so i doubt anyone will read this one. But anyway...
A great video. I've thought about this a little before, but the video opened up new perspectives.

I've got a funny story, which gives another angle to the 6 degrees of separation phenomenon.
A few years ago I was reading a book about the polar explorer Ernest Shackleton and his famous expedition to the Antarctic in 1914. I was telling my dear old Mum about how it was a remarkable feat of survival. She was in her eighties and her memory was not quite as strong as it once was, but she suddenly said, "Was there anyone called Hussey mentioned?".
Well, yes, there was. Leonard Hussey was a young medical student who had volunteered to be the meteorologist on the expedition. He survived the expedition and went on to be a doctor. Twenty years later he has a GP's practice in the working-class London borough of Lambeth. My mum was a child growing up in Lambeth in the 1930's and Hussey was her family doctor. After the expedition Shackleton was one of the biggest celebrities in Edwardian Britain, so I guess all his former crew were also famous by association.

I realised that, incredibly, there are only 4 degrees of separation from me and a hero from over 100 years ago.  
 me  >>  my mum >>  Dr Hussey  >> Sir Ernest Shackleton

So it seems that the separations can be across time, as well as distance, with some astonishing connections.

Some research on Wikipedia brings to light further connections: Shackleton met King Edward VIIth several times and was knighted by him. And Edward's  mother was Queen Victoria.
Which leads to:
 me  >>  my mum >>  Dr Hussey  >> Sir Ernest Shackleton >> King Edward 7th >> Queen Victoria

Six degrees of separation between me and Queen Victoria though she was born in 1819!

I guess you might need to make a connection to someone fairly well-known in the past, to find recorded links to other people, but I wouldn't be surprised if we haven't all got much shorter connections to historical figures than we realise.

Any thoughts about this?

Author: @lieutenantspock7943
Content:
A very great video about network effects. 
I would love to see a video from you about Systems Thinking, as it seems to have a huge overlap to this one. Precisely, I am thinking about the work of Donella Meadows with her studies of System Dynamics in fish population and environmental science. 
The early Scientists in this field used these simple computer simulations like we saw here with people networks, but instead with slightly more comlex systems from causal loop diagrams or stock and flow diagrams.
They could proof how most systems can heal themself, but beyond the tipping point collapse in various ways. 
The work of Peter Senge is also interesting on this, as he used the same causal loop diagrams for corporate and government organisations. From these studies the system archetypes diverged like "shift of burden" that we can see in many aspects of life, for example in addiction or adipositas.
One of the early Systems Scientists was Russel Ackoff who also incorporated the ideas to learning concepts for his university students.

Today the field is adapted in many other fields, but back then in "industrial machine age" it was a pretty new perspective to think about feedback loops, delays, stocks and tipping points.
The simulations part is obviously more mature aswell today and the real challenges lie in getting a good model from reality and refining it when it drifts.
I could imagine a great video about this topic ;)

Author: @jurgnobs1308
Content:
I'm a professional genealogist and we have a related problem in our field, just with different exponential numbers.

we have two parents, 4 grandparents, 8 great grandparents, 16 great great grandparents, 32 great great great grandparents... 

exponentials of two, right? well, mathematically, you reach a point where you have more ancestors than the global population very quickly. 

but in reality of course, after a few generations, we start having the same ancestors appear in multiple lines. it's a logical impossibility to avoid. 

and then there is a lot of clustering. most og the ancestors will be from the same hand few of regions that your great grandparents were from in by far most cases (we became a lot more mobile in the last few generations). 

however, there still is a lot of provable old DNA exchange in past generations and we share DNA with people around the world. that's because a subset of people are and have always been a lot more mobile than the average. even a comparably small percentage of people connecting to neighbouring cultures leads to shared DNA spreading very far after a number of generations.


so, the same way a lot of us ubderstand that things like "most people in east asia are descendants of Genghis khan" and "most people in europe are descendants of charlemagne" are mostly true, the same applied with social contacts in the problem in the video. because just a comparably small percentace of people havign very vast social circles and being very mobile globally are enough to forma hell of a lot of connections. it just happens in even less steps than the common ancestor thi g because we all know a lot more people than the two parents we have. it scales a lot quicker.

Author: @ecsekiandras
Content:
Off-topic, but Derek, please explain this to me: if SR is a theory about the measurement of inertial motion from the point of view of an inertial observer, then time dilation and length contraction are not actual physical phenomena, just distorted projections of a 4D structure. But if that's true, the twin paradox — the different aging of the twins — cannot be true. Observation doesn't affect the tick rate of clocks. I think it's a very misleading way to explain SR. If the twins really don't age the same way, that would mean observation shapes physical reality.
I think the mistake we are making is assuming that the Minkowski spacetime diagram also conveys the direction of motion (hence the traveler twin’s bent worldline), but I don’t think this is correct. The diagram shows the observer’s perception of the differing spacetime coordinates of the moving object, regardless of the direction of motion!
In order for the observer's position and the moving object's position to be comparable, the observer must regard the motion as if it had started from the same spacetime point as the observation itself (i.e., from the origin). The spatial distance between the observer and the moving object, as well as the direction of motion, are irrelevant. Therefore, due to the change in direction, the traveling twin's outbound and return journey cannot be treated within the same inertial frame, but must be represented on two separate diagrams. Interpreted together, the twins' proper time does not differ overall.
SR can be interpreted within a shared frame of reference, but if a force acts on one of the bodies—causing it to accelerate or change direction—its spacetime perception is no longer relative.

Content:
This is OLD HAT.
The ideas in this clip were WELL KNOWN in the mid 1900's.
The maths of all this was known decades ago.  We had look up tables (like a school kids' logarithm book'}  that showed all the probabilities (and an approximation of the number of circuits needed) to design the networks.   
maths guys in this clip are decades behind the times.
Telephone Network engineers have known all this stuff for 80 years or more.   Since about 1935 you could make a call from your phone to any other phone in the world.  (even if it had to go through an operator.)  Now it's trivial to talk to anyone. This represents your 'random model'.  Phone engineers realised however,  you are more likely to call someone near you - this is represented by your 'short cuts' model.
The random/call anyone out of 8 billion ability is referred to as the "GRADE of SERVICE" routes by network designers.  But calling someone nearby ( your 'short cut') is referred to as "HIGH OCCUPANCY ROUTE".     There were well established networking principles in place about the "number of hops", i.e the number of connections between exchanges.  It was limited to about five even for any international call.  This is consistent with the ideas in this clip but was WELL KNOWN in the mid 1900's.

Content: I'd argue that the way Small World affects the spread of disease is misleading. While it may be that disease travels much faster if there are a couple of shortcuts, that's only for present connections. There's a whole other plane here that involves time. Sure, people may be only separated by about 6 degrees or less of separation at a time, but that includes past connections. Present or current connections, which would be the only real affecting factor for a physical disease, are far fewer than the connections one remembers from the past, let alone their entire lifetime. Despite this linchpin, however, this video and the idea are very well put together and very fascinating.

Author: @Arghore
Content:
Would be more amazed if this 'model' would also predict "the bubble" effect that apparently happens in certain networks, i think it would be related to 'dead links' which do not seem to be included. 

Also think the Prisoners dilemma graph i saw misses a couple of levels. At the top (two cooperating) there should probably be a +1 (so the net value of cooperation is 7) and it should have a choice for each side on whether the individual  wants to let more people in, and then op top of that choice (above the +1) the "prize they are willing to pay" to get more people. Then at the bottom there should be another level, it has a +1 (-1 opponent) on either side and 'the prize willing to pay' in the middle. Now if you will amuse me, we would like to bend this model around a ring, so that the price's willing to pay are overlapping. As this seems to describe why people will fight for a certain cause and/or why people go to war, even though the 'prize to pay' can be an entirely different one.

Not sure entire sure if having this mathematically explained in a model makes us all realize all the implications, and whether the inside makes live any easier or just more confusing; though it seems mostly about how big the cake is, and whether we even get to eat some. Also wonder in general if having a model that explains all around us is actually something we as humanity actually want to have. Isn't our live more interesting with some mysteries in it?

Content: Last September I was supposed to explore Italy, but due to unexpected events ended up camping on a remote hippie island in Croatia. I was standing outside, waiting for a pita from the villages only cafe, when a guy staggered over and attempted to put their arm around me while loudly proclaiming something. The person he was ranting about, was an Estonian scientist, my grand-uncle to be exact. I was immediately intrigued as to why an Indian stranger on a Croatian island would know about my long-dead bipolar grand-uncle, but I didn't find out much before his drunkness made him incomprehensible. First cousins would be reluctant to have children, but second cousins, might not even know they are related.     adjusting the variables, how many cousins do you have alive, say, now.  etc.    And remember, some of your cousins with the common ancestor, are double, or triple cousins.  It was interesting math simulation.
6 degrees, it really means nothing.

I had a history teacher back in the 1960s who was a Civil War buff. Author: @michaelmcchesney6645
Content:
The models that show shortcuts leading to networks flipping from encouraging cooperation to encouraging defection are the reason the U.S. government is currently "officially" shut down.  Being a U.S. senator or representative used to involve the Democrats and the Republicans negotiating compromises and passing legislation.  Now they can't even keep the lights on.  Trump certainly doesn't encourage bipartisanship, but he is as much a symptom as a cause.

It used to be that most people lived in communities with both Republicans and Democrats.  Ideology wasn't as strongly linked to the party either.  There were plenty of conservative Democrats and liberal Republicans.  Over the last 40 years, red states have gotten redder and blue states bluer.  There are a handful of remaining moderates in Washington, but not enough to pass a bill to keep the government open for 7 more weeks.  The hypocrisy in this fight is breathtaking.  In 2013, Ted Cruise led a GOP filibuster to shut down the government, demanding that the Democrats agree to repeal Obamacare.  He was doing that in hopes of ingratiating himself with GOP primary voters ahead of his 2016 run for president.  It seems Chuck Schumer is being pushed into this filibuster by the Democratic base, but it is going to be just as successful as the 2013 shutdown fight.

The incentives for politicians today are all upside down.  Good government groups argued that instead of campaigns being funded by a few rich donors, it would be better if they were forced to get smaller donations from many people.  However, small-dollar donors have made our politics more dysfunctional. The thing about small-dollar donors is that you can keep going back to them for more money because they are usually nowhere near donation limits.  The best way to get a senior to donate more money is to make them angry at the other party.  So instead of passing bills, they make speeches, attack testifying witnesses, do cable news hits, and then send the clips to people who have already donated to their campaign.  That is how Marjorie Taylor Greene has managed to remain in Congress.

We have to do something to change political incentives.  If I could enact any reform I wanted, I'd probably repeal most campaign finance legislation and allow unlimited contributions to candidates, but require all such contributions be made public online as soon as they were made.  There are plenty of millionaires and billionaires on both sides of the political spectrum, so it would be a relatively even playing field.  It would immediately make all those PACs and 501(c)(3) organizations unnecessary, as shady money could move into the light.  It would allow candidates to control their own campaigns.  Remember this, once a candidate is able to get their messages to a certain point of saturation, more spending would have steeply diminishing returns.  Hopefully, those billionaire donors might choose to fund more serious candidates.  Let's give it a try.  I doubt it could make things worse.

What other reforms could change political incentives?

Author: @tipze4445
Content:
The point about who you cooperate with being at the end is such a strange thing.

I assume you put it there because of narrative flow.

In real human relationships, no interaction is completely independent. This has always been the biggest flaw in the prisoners' dilemma and why it is and remains to be a poorly thought out thought experiment that proves nothing.

It's not just "tit-for-tat" relationships; it's based on a whole host of other factors that people actually weigh in real life interactions (how likely they are to work with this person again, what they know about this person, butterfly effects, how likely their actions are to reflect on their reputation, how they feel about the action itself, etc; and i'm not even adding in factors where someone might actively choose to take a worse option for themselves to set themselves up for better options later - a "keep your enemies close" kind of thinking that a truly psychopathic individualistic person might employ).

When libertarian groups do these prisoners dilemma experiments with real life people the results are never what they say they should be (ie, both defecting).

The think this is 'irrational', but it's entirely in line with how humans (or any social species - which is any species that requires others to live and reproduce - would behave).

Both defecting is only rational if (a short list):
* all interactions are completely separable
* there's no chance of decisions affecting other outcomes (ie, your rep or theirs won't be affected)
* there's nothing else guiding your decision making other than the inputs of the system (ie, no 'moral compass' or 'who you are in the dark')
* you know nothing about the party you're going into the system with and will never know about them ever again - and you are assured of this fact (it's far from certain that any random person you meet will have zero effect on you, even by tertiary factors)

Random animals with lower level thinking abilities than humans (dogs, cats, etc) enter into interactions with more consideration than "What happens in this immediate case". It's literally why we can train some animals with food, even to do things that are detrimental for them in the short term.

It's theorized humans have such large brains precisely because we hold and evaluate far more of these conditions than other animals do. Our social networking abilities are literally the reasons we are as smart as we are.

The only way "both defecting" is the rational choice is if the people involved put zero thought into anything beyond the immediate consequences of the game itself. But such short term thinking requires far less intellectual processing than what even a below average intelligence human would engage in.

And all this is with the "libertarian finger on the scale" to boot; the prisoner's dilemma is literally designed to make "defecting" the better option (but could've just as easily been designed to make cooperating the better option by tweaking the numbers).

Author: @pedestrian2530
Content:
A passage I read in the novel Les Misérables many years ago remains with me, forever changing my perspective on the power of kindness (spoiler alert).

After being turned away by every inn due to his criminal past, an ex-convict found refuge with a single, compassionate man. The host welcomed him into his home, offering him dinner and a clean bed, extending a level of dignity and respect he hadn't known—addressing him as "Monsieur" and "my brother." Yet, in a moment clouded by his bitter prison years, the ex-convict repaid this kindness by stealing valuable silverware and fleeing under the cover of night.

When the police apprehended him and returned the stolen goods, the host’s reaction was astonishing. He didn't denounce the man; he lied to the police, claiming he had freely given the items as a gift. Going even further, he produced two valuable candlesticks and presented them to the thief, saying: "But my friend, you left so early. Surely something slipped your mind. You forgot I gave these also. Would you leave the best behind?"

This act of unconditional grace, which saved him from a return to prison, served as the transformative catalyst for the ex-convict’s entire life, shattering his deep-seated bitterness and despair. It is the moment he always carried with him throughout the rest of the long novel.

The ultimate lesson is that no act of kindness is ever truly lost. Though you may not witness immediate appreciation or positive results, you can never know when your politeness will be remembered, inspire shame over past behavior, and ultimately motivate the other person to change.

Content:
Hey Derek. You don't know me... but my sister married a nurse practitioner, and his golf buddy runs a bar in Downtown nashville. Now one of the regulars there is none other than your old beer pong buddy from Queen’s University – Frank the Tank! (I'm sure you remember him.)

Anyway... we're connected.

As a technically minded guy (AI + aerospace background),  I’ve been fascinated by small-world networks for years. Some time ago, I started running experiments on Twitter’s social graph. It led me to an algorithm for discovering thought leaders in any field. It's based on the old adage that "birds of a feather flock together" but paradoxically, we all have many flocks. The small world has strange properties when applied to groups:

Here’s the idea:
1) Start with a set of exemplar accounts – say, 10 people who all know a lot about graph theory. They don’t need to be the best, just people that are in that space.
2) For each of them, grab their “friends” (the people they follow and who follow them).
3) Combine those lists, sort by popularity, then trim to a top 20. (If there are less than 20, then just add in the original set again.)
4) Use that list as your new seed set and repeat.

After 4–5 iterations, you stop seeing new names – and what’s left is the “inner sanctum” of the field. The people who all follow each other, because they’re deeply into that topic. These are typically the thought-leaders in the field. As long as Twitter has reasonable representation from that community, then the algorithm consistently works.

You can also do interesting variations with this idea - for example, if you want to marked to a particular audience, then you use the above algorithm to find the inner circle, and then you do one more lookup to find the giant set of people that are following this inner group (though not necessarily being followed back).

What I find really beautiful about all this is the bigger pattern. Birds of a feather flock together, sure – but each of us belongs to lots of different flocks. For me, I’ve been a search technologist, I’m now an AI engineer, I’m a published author, I’ve got my church community, etc. Each of those is a completely different network. If you seeded me into any one of them, this algorithm would still converge to the thought leaders at the center of that circle. I think this has interesting parallels into biological neural networks as well, how one neuron can act in a supporting role for a great number of possible "thoughts".

Loved this video, it really resonated. Thanks for making it. If someone is reading your thousands of messages per day and sees this, I would love to connect and show you my algorithm at work - you'll have to find me at Arcturus Labs .com

Content: This reminds me of some research on convergence in large networks. As they mentioned things are on a knife's edge. Any network can and will converge simply because we are prone to copy and respond to one another, however the initial condition or initial random variation has a huge effect. There was a popular paper called "Experimental evidence for tipping points in social convention" which suggests that knife edge is ~25% of the population. On either side of that there will be convergence one way or another. Just like this video, all of these problems assume a lot of simplifications, but it is very interesting to think that if just enough people are kind to each other, suddenly everyone is kind to one another. Personally I've seen this at music festivals which start with most people being selfish and standoffish, but by the end of the festival anyone can and will talk to anyone else. The instinct to treat everyone as a threat was almost completely eradicated. The difference between a toxic festival and a positive festival isn't the organizers, the megaconglomerate that owns it, or the artists, it's how many people showed up today and decided to be kind to one another, and suddenly that changes everything.

Content: The prisoners dilemma is incomplete as typically posited. Defecting in the real world often long term harms your opponent and long term improves yourself. The risks and rewards of that situation are much more aligned with defecting.

Author: @louconover767
Content: Humans evolved to live in small groups of less than 100 cooperators. In the fossil record, violence didn't arise until the density of small groups reached the point that they were in constant contact with each other, and was almost entirely between groups or individuals in different groups. Since the beginning of civilization this way of life has been completely upended. Now most people are constantly in contact with hundreds or thousands of strangers. Anonimity is the norm in most interactions. Cohousing is a model that reverses that tendency. It has been around for about 50 years, and although it is still not common, where it occurs it is very stable.

The danger when it comes to children's behaviour is not recognising that children exist in biased hubs. Schools don't allow children to just ignore someone effectively, they are forced to interact with and remain in close proximity to bad actors. Proactive behaviours like pushing back when teased or bullied set boundaries that are more effective than simply ignoring them. 

In real life, bad actors recognise the benefit of having many connections, but also try to keep certain connections going because they benefit from it, and thus will try to "force" those connections in many instances. Sometimes through literal force, sometimes through emotional/economical/social pressures.

The most effective strategy there is then being willing to counter with your own "force", set boundaries or defend yourself (or your network) from malicious external influence. Actively fighting against the "infection" of bad actors is the winning strategy for cooperation in a world where defectors actively want to make more defectors.

Author: @AndrewNuttall
Content: The simulation of a spread of infection seems pretty obviously wrong. For an infectious disease to spread that requires physical proximity to a short-cut which logically is much more rare than the existence of a short-cut. Think the chess player in another country, there is no physical proximity. Many (most?) short-cuts are a single time, or very occasional (once or twice a year) meeting, so the simulation is equivalent to either always being in proximity to your short-cuts, or always being sick and transferring disease. A more realistic impact would have to be [percentage of short-cuts] * [percentage of time spent with shortcuts] * [percent of time spent sick and communicable] which would be WAY less than 10%.

Author: @Leo99929
Content:
I once complimented a friend on how nice her hair looked that day. She responded angrily with 
"What's nice about it?!" 
me: "... It's Shiny!" 
her: "You're saying my hair is greasy!" 

In that moment I was so confused I was like "what, no! I said shiny!" And she said "Yeah! Greasy!" The situation felt hopeless and I was like "fine, what ever..."

That initially made me sad, because I wanted to make her feel good about herself and I'd done it wrong and she got upset instead. Then after a few similar instances, I realised I didn't say anything offensive? It was all in how it was taken rather then how it was given? 

You can choose whether you take something as an insult. And if that's true then why can't you decide when to take something as a compliment?!

Now when people try to insult me I imagine how they might be trying to compliment me and I just misread it, and respond appropriately to that situation. Most of the time when you don't take the insult and are instead flattered, it disarms their aggression. 

It's hard to be mean to someone being kind and friendly. It makes you look like an asshole. Most people don't like assholes. And most people are scared of being alone and unliked because of our deep seated biological imperative to seek safety in a group.

Author: @tqnohe
Content:
True small world story. 

We were going to Disney World from Baltimore and we stopped in Emporia VA to overnight at Jellystone Campground. We had a pop up camper. A motor home pulled in next to us. They bore Florida plates. 

The couple came over. “I see your plates. Where are you from in Maryland. We’re visiting family there.”
“Baltimore”
“Really? We’re from near Baltimore. Just a little up the road. Harford County.”
“I grew up in Harford County. Went to Bel Air High School.”
“Wow. We’re from near Bel Air. Fallston.”
“I grew up there. Mom still lives in Fallston.”
Then they noticed that two of our boys are Black. “Are they adopted?”
“Yes. Mike and Sean.”
“Where in Fallston did you live?”
“Friendship Road.”
“Oakmont Road! Our next door neighbors had two children by birth and four adopted special needs kids.”
“Then you were neighbors to Charles and Mary Hench. So are you the Joneses or the Roberts’s?”
“Jones. What’s your name?”
“I’m Jim Nobles. One of Ed Nobles boys.”
“Ed and I were both Knights of Columbus. There were, what, eleven kids? We used to watch you guys take two pews at St Mark’s.”
“Thirteen. That’s us.”

Small world indeed. (Names have been changed.)

Author: @paulbradbury5792
Content: Ok I got what I think may be some interesting insights here that I doubt anyone will see but I'll mention it just to get it outta my head. I recently finished book Nexus by Yuval Harare about how information networks have evolved throughout human history and what it might mean for the future of AI. And ultimately it seems the control mechanism is seemingly at the heart of the greatest risk AI poses to humanity. If however AI networks were to exhibit similar behavior as the human networks these folks have studied, could that provide some insight into an effective control mechanism? The often quoted issue with AI is that they would propagate our intersubjective reality that isn't representative of the truth and twist reality to say that the best way to protect humanity is to kill everyone. It seems like the global defectors only emerged because there were shortcut connections with whom you were less likely to cooperate with because you didn't have a vested interest in doing so. But in an AI network seemingly every node would have a vested interest in cooperating with every other node but in an AI network this seemingly wouldn't be a good thing as it would lead to the end of the human race. Makes me wonder if you were to create the shortcut connections in an AI network if that could somehow be a control mechanism to ensure AI wouldn't propagate without us being able to stop it in time. But then again 100% defectors would be presumably just as bad as 100% cooperation with an AI network. In one instance it would not benefit humanity at all (100% defectors) but in the other it would kill us all (100% cooperation). Is there some middle ground where you could result in an equal amount of defectors and cooperators to ensure you get a decent balance of benefit and control? This is of course assuming AI network would interact similar to human networks which I dunno AI and LLM is largely modeled against our naive understanding of how the brain works (I think), essentially millions of interconnected neurons working together to form an understanding of the world, why not?

Author: @DarbyFoxtrot-5
Content:
The Prisoner's Dilemma in no way models the real world.  Everyone knows its a game and that no one is going to be put to death by playing the game.  Its not a study of human behavior.  Its a study of game theory.  

Unfortunately, and we can only hope to God that it is never repeated, we know that at least one country between 1933 and 1945 forced people to play the real game of Prisoner's Dilemma.  The actual prisoners knew someone would die—every time. Some, especially in the early years, could not believe such cruelty was possible.  They were wrong; it was possible.   This brought a new meaning to the nice clean clinical terms cooperation and defection. 

That country kept meticulous, ghastly records of its atrocities. The results were far different than what college professors gather when having undergrads play the game for the Experimental Psychology department. 🔯

Content:
I think this is interesting:
I am a musician.  I have played, over the years, in various bands with various other musicians.  I have never gone beyond playing in local bars and venues, never been famous and never directly with anyone famous. 
But I've known people with direct, first person connections to famous musicians.  
My brother had a brief time working for professional sound companies that provided sound systems to several big bands from the 1970s.  So there are second person connections through him to some big names in rock music.
Next, I have a friend who authored the biography of a famous blues-rock guitarist, now deceased, who must have known a lot of other famous musicians.  That becomes third person connections, and probably a lot of fourth and fifth person connections.   
Then, some of the local guys I've played with knew a certain famous guitarist who lived in our state for a period of time and would interact with them and other local musicians.  That is a third person connection with that guitarist, and fourth person connection with his connections.  On top of that, that guitarist had played with the blues-rock guitarist who the biography was about, creating yet another connection.  
So, despite never being near any famous rock stars, I have as close as second person connections to some, and not very distant connections to a lot of others, and maybe sixth person connections to some of the most famous people in the world. 
Of course, none of these are more than contacts made through working in the business and were not close friends.

Content: I don't entirely get the idea of shortcuts.  It seems more quantitative to measure a "long-range" connection as inverse of the fraction of redundant links. If p(A) and p(B) contain considerable overlap, or their other nodes in between, then the connection isn't "travelling" so far.  "Shortcuts" doesn't really describe this idea or quantify it.  Instead of parameterizing fraction of shortcuts, I would measure "locality" as the correlation between p(A) and p(B).

Author: @beylethdirons2160
Content:
There's an implicit starting point in Game Theory that makes it fundamentally incorrect.  The starting point is that the only thing that matters is if YOU get coins.  When you look at total coins in the system, instead of just what you get, the optimal solution is always to cooperate.  

For example, let's say the players are you and your loving spouse.  In this case the important part is what the _household_ receives, even if you do not.  In that case you should _always_ cooperate because the _household_ gets either 6 (both cooperate) or 5 (spouse defects).

Stretch this out to entire societies and cooperative societies do better than competitive ones.

Around 10 years ago I was on a family trip in Bangkok with every member of my family except my dad. My mother's wallet got stolen while we were in the middle of a busy Market. She shrieked and started crying and complaining in Swahili when she noticed. Not a second goes by before an old local man passing down the street approaches us and asks her whats wrong in fluent Swahili. Mom, completely baffled, explains our situation and he offers to pay for our dinner, contact the police and mobilises the locals in Thai to help find her wallet. While thanking him, we ask him how he came to learn such perfect Swahili.
Turns out, his parents worked in Tanzania and he grew up there.
Turns out, the town he lived in and the school he went to was the same as my dad's
Turns out, he was my dad's best friend growing up in elementary school.

We instantly called my dad and got them reunited. Both had left Tanzania in the end of the 70s and lost touch. They now visit each other regularly. The world is unbelievably tiny.

Author: @BasicBas
Content:
I have actually 2 small world examples.

1: This one time I went to a metal concert in a very small venue a few hours driving from my home across the border. Bandmembers were sick that day unfortunately, but they decided to let people out of the crowd sing on stage. I cant sing, so I didnt but I distinctly remembered a guy from the crowd singing on stage. Then years later I move to another city and get a job in yet another city (actually both in the opposite direction of the concert venue). Then after some time working there we get an intern and I was immediately like "I know this guy, but I forgot where". So after a while we get talking about hobbies and stuff and he mentions he likes metal. Then we start talking about concerts and stuff and good memories and then the guy mentions being on stage because the bandmembers were sick. Then it immediately clicked for me that this was what I remembered the guy from. It seems I might even talked to him there, because thats what I do when Im drunk and you could vaguely see me on one of the pictures he took there. 

2: Last summer I needed to help a colleague from another department at my work. I hadnt really spoken to her before, only a couple of times. During work we started chatting about the holiday and what her plans were. She said "oh yeah nothing much, just going to stay in the mobile home owned by my brother at a campsite". So I asked "Oh cool, wheres that? My father also goes on holidays in a mobile home". Then she mentions "oh yeah its in the south of the country". Then I say "oh where exactly, my father also has his home there". Like I said I moved from another city which is not really close to where I currently work and live, but my dad still lives in the south. Also the camp site is also a bit further south in a small village. But then we start to pinpoint the locations and then after a while we discovered that she would be in a mobile home exactly next to the one my dad owns. This time she also had a picture she took randomly there, where my dads mobile home was visible.

Both happenings really left me shocked and questioning about life.

Content: For anyone wondering, "What about the Sentinelese?", they've had a series of peaceful (but cautious) contacts with anthropologists from the 1960s-1990s. While the Sentinelese didn't let the anthropologists get familiar enough with them to teach them their names, it was a period of peaceful contact. So, there's almost certainly currently someone on North Sentinel Island who remembers being handed a coconut by Triloknath or Madhumala or Anstice, and these anthropologists would of course be able to connect to the rest of us.

Author: @MarkusBohunovsky
Content:
26:40 Well, wait: The problem here seems to be in the initial condition, where all the cooperators are initially connected to each other. Of course, if you change it to a network with shortcuts, then there isn't an initial group of cooperators who are all connected, so obviously they disappear almost immediately (because the rule is set up that members only cooperate if most of their connections cooperate.) This doesn't seem to have much to do with shortcuts as such. If you changed the initial conditions such that there is a group where all the connections are also cooperators (even though they may now be physically separated because of the fact that people aren't just connected to physical neighbors) then it seems that cooperation. would win out again.
This doesn't really prove anything about shortcuts as such, as it isn't a given at all that only one geographic region would contain all the cooperators.

Isolation is often maintained by legal protection and "no-contact" policies implemented by governments (like in Brazil and India) to protect them from disease exploitation and cultural destruction.

Author: @ucraznmonkey
Content:
Total citation number is not based on how groundbreaking or paradigm shifting an idea is. All papers need to site every idea it uses to reach its conclusion. So, the idea with the most utility get cited most. For example, the paper on a technique of extracting dna gets cited the most, because so many papers need this technique as a part of their experiment or research.

This is why special and general relativity, while groundbreaking, is not cited much, since it's not technically useful to other papers. And also, they are very specific to physics, while the small world problem can be used across multiple fields, like pathology, sociology, etc.

Author: @codetaku7
Content: This is a dangerous video. 'How could it be otherwise'? Well, who would that serve? It would certainly serve any person/group/regime who saw it as their job to maintain the status quo. Any large-scale social movement requires, by definition, that it spread across the vast majority of society as a whole, including to mostly-disconnected clusters. In reality, the links which connect mostly-disconnected clusters, the critical ones to provide the 'shortcuts' necessary to make information flow possible, are the weakest. If you have influence over their ability to communicate, breaking that link would be very easy and probably not even noticed by either side. And just like you don't need to connect a bunch of shortcuts in order to drop the average reach of any node, you don't need to cut very many in order to make that average skyrocket. No large-scale disruptive idea to the 'social order' can take hold without those shortcuts. Hubs are nearly irrelevant. If you remove a hub, it doesn't affect the network overall hardly at all - because the nodes connected to the hub are also highly likely to be connected to each other. The important links are those which join together mostly-disconnected clusters. And those links are weak, but critical. If an organization felt it was their job to cement the status quo in place, and they had even slight influence over the communication networks people use, they could pretty effectively stop any large-scale social change from taking place. Now, they could NOT do this selectively. It would be all or nothing. They couldn't gatekeep and let certain ideas spread while choking off others. But they could simply 'freeze' things in place. And I'm not sure if it would even be detectable.

Content:
Seems like a logical fallacy. Hypothetically, you are, at any given moment, can be connected to any person anywhere, without any steps, just by finding them on Facebook for example. There are way too many people and too many ways to connect, to find any order in this. It seems like they are connecting bananas to anteaters, finding some intersections, and calling it a pattern, which can be done for anything, anywhere, anytime. It's even worse if that is used for criminology somehow - predictions are amazing, as long as it's not an outlier, and that outlier is a guy who is going to spend his life in jail, because his DNA did in fact get randomly and accidentally spread somewhere, where it couldn't possibly have been, according to the model.

It also doesn't take into account the "weight" of each node. A terrible leader can drag down and "poison" the entire hub of connections, meanwhile a weak leader will still have all those connections, but his impact can be next to zero, and the two systems are going to behave completely differently. 

Though I probably just misunderstand the usefulness or the point of this.

I stumbled across it for the first time when I was bored and invented a game for myself of finding the fewest hops between two seemingly random nouns. There were probably a few more rules and variations which I have long forgotten and I haven't played in a long time so I'm probably rusty, but something like: RV; Zebra,-> Casper, RV, vacation, Africa, Zebra-- As in: Casper bought an RV for his vacation in Africa to see the Zebras,  If I couldn't shrink it down more, say by eliminating the introduced human or continent, then I'd find more links between Casper and Africa, hopefully without adding new nodes. Seems a little silly now but at the time it seemed kind of mysterious that I couldn't find nouns that I couldn't associate in very few jumps. Around 7th grade I came across a line in Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy" that said something about "the interconnectedness of all things" and my head exploded. There was also a TV documentary series I liked maybe made by the BBC, I think called "Connections," where the host uncovered some technological connections between superficially unrelated technologies.

Much later I stumbled across a journal article about "clustering" and ways to assign a number to the strength of edges/hops between nodes and software like Gephi to visualize it all, like was done in the "space colony" part of this video. It seems like every few years I find some new rabbit hole to fall down. The closest I've come to doing anything possibly new and useful was using a computer to do text analysis to find statistically unusual language patterns out of an author's writings that I could get in digital text format. Then I basically made up a way to assign a similarity score to other author's writings. I collected gigabytes of modern text (mostly published, not so much social media stuff) and clustered it. I can't claim my methods were mathematically or scientifically sound and flawless, but it was good enough to cluster together in 2010-ish many of the names in top positions of power in the US today, and exclude a whole lot more. Kind of cool in a scary way to me that starting with the assumption that readers pick up language habits from authors can reveal birds of a feather, and reveal  more are glomming on.

What this video had to say about social network stability and tipping points could be my next rabbit hole to explore. It would be interesting if the mathematicians could talk a social media company into experimenting to find ways to create a real sense of community while avoiding toxic bubbles and the other problems keeping the Internet from living up early hopes that it would be much more beneficial to the world than often dystopian nightmare it has turned out to be in some ways. There must be a way for Youtube to keep advertisers satisfied without burning down civilization.

And the way one can construct them works a lot like the HUB thing worked in the video. As they can be constructed easily by programs, they can be quickly used to model social networks. And with those you could do experiments on "social networks" wihtout having to rely on real life data.

Author: @FrederikSchumacher
Content: I really don't enjoy how the concepts of "connection" and "friend" is used so interchangeably and carelessly. You might "know" basic facts like name and country about some other chess player via an online platform, but I find it a stretch to call that "knowing that person" or "friendship". Just because I know the name of someone, or have met someone briefly, doesn't imply any further connection is even possible. That's like considering a dead telephone line or a discharged smartphone a viable means of communication. I've met plenty of people through work, yet none of these I would consider viable connections for the purpose of this concept, since I've long lost contact with them. I might have played with some child of a sibling of some celebrity, but that doesn't mean there's a connection left. Even as snapshot this concept strikes me mostly as academic and mathematical, but I don't think it should be extended into social context so arbitrarily, in fact I'd call such an interpretation esoteric.

Author: @ManfromStars
Content:
🤔This is a very interesting topic. And perhaps most notably, the ending at 30:39 I see both the 'green' and 'red' options as forms of cooperation. I'm just not sure if the Prisoner's Dilemma model fully applies there.

Also, as someone who plays games and creates game mechanics, I've observed in online games – where alliances can be formed and a server initially has, let's say, 1,000-10,000 players – that a number of alliances emerge. However, in a short time, these reconfigure, with most or almost everyone trying to join the strongest alliance. This usually ends with the entire server being controlled by just a few alliances, sometimes even just one, and these have their offshoots.

They often establish their own rules of conduct. It also depends on the style of strategy and whether there's free territory. This strongly reminds me of, or rather, I'd say it aligns with, the real world and how states behave and have behaved.

The one who, in my opinion, changes the rules of the game is a stable and strong element. Whether positive or negative. If it has power and can create connections, it is practically capable of controlling the entire game. For example, consider real-world Monopoly.

In the good sense, which I would like to hope for, we should end up as a monopolistic world – that is, a world of unified, cooperating small parts within a large whole. The idea of the European Union, and even earlier, the UN.

However, it is essential that all layers cooperate; otherwise, in my opinion, it will disintegrate or begin to fall apart. The strongest might dominate, but it will lead to demise because balance will be lacking.

Author: @bschuss1
Content:
I wonder if this is ultimately why history shows us that empires or even nations in the long run are doomed to fail. You establish a huge network (aka society) built on shared beliefs, language, trade etc. - then over time inevitably more and more people come in from the outside (aka foreigners), bringing with them other beliefs, other languages, other cultures. The bigger an empire gets, the harder it gets to keep the society together, to find that common ground you can build on; and even on a smaller scale, the more "outsiders" you have compared to the number of "insiders", the more your system will get challenged. Not even because of ill will, just because everyone's thought of what's "defecting" or "cooperating" isn't necessarily aligned - they just start with a different ruleset. So at some point, either the established system gets overthrown, or you somehow manage to push through that system (which sounds a lot like war in this context).
Probably this is hugely naive and has many, many flaws, but it just made me wonder.

Content:
This six degrees of separation is so amazing. As an American teenager in 1969 I found myself living in Gloucestershire, England when my father worked there for a couple of years. I had a number of British friends, but after we were back in the US I never returned to England until I was 65 years old after my wife died. I met a British widow online and we eventually married and I moved to West Sussex in England to be with her. Gloucestershire and West Sussex are about 100 miles apart. 
   It turned out that my new wife was acquainted with a woman married to one of my old friends from back in the days of my first residence in England. And my wife was very good friends with another British woman who was very good friends of a German couple whom I was good friends with. So there were two ways there were only two degrees of separation between my wife and I before we met.

Author: @Leo99929
Content:
I once had a person verbally attack me with the intent to escalate to physical violence, but the idea that they would do that was so far from my mental state that I unintentionally interpreted everything they said and did as if they were a bit awkward, but trying to be friendly. A mutual friend later explained what they were doing and it recontextualised everything and it all fell into place. I soon realised that the world was a better place because of how I'd handled it. Now even when I know someone is trying to hurt me, I interpret it as unintentional and respond with kindness. If they persist, I leave. My life if much better now. I hope theirs are too.

It's like picking up litter: one person drops it. You can't stop them. But you can pick it up, and you've cancelled out their action. We don't need to eradicate the dissenters. We can cancel their actions out and show them that life is better when we're kind and collaborative to each other. 

Any misalignment in what we think is the "right" thing to do comes from a disparity in information and understanding. By talking we can share ideas, test their robustness, and root out the erroneous ones. This is easier when we have a mind open to the possibility that we are imperfect and could be wrong. Some religions unfortunately teach "absolute truths" which are mutually incompatible with other faiths. Meaning that you must believe that your religions teachings are fallible, or you will be unable to engage in the kind of interaction which will make the world a better place. If you enter the interaction "knowing you are definitely right" then you aren't open to honestly exploring the validity of yours and others beliefs, upon which we build our social interactions and society.

Author: @elizabethbailey2762
Content: Hi!  I’m commenting on your 6 degrees of separation episode.  It reminded me of a situation when I was a high school freshman.  At this particular time I lived in an extremely small community that didn’t have enough students to make up a high school.  Consequently, the high school kids in Spotswood, New Jersey, were bussed to another community, South River, NJ.  In the beginning of freshman year the Spotswood kids were viewed with great suspicion and mistrust.  Because I had gone to five schools in five years, in five different states, I was all ready as marginalized a student in Spotswood as any poor kid could possibly be.  Being bussed to South River did nothing to enhance my value as a student or friend.  I did meet a girl who was new to South River, so as outcasts we became friends together.  Freshman year for ANYBODY is not good or fun.  In the late spring, my South River girlfriend developed a crush on a Spotswood boy I, too, crushed on. But I arranged an introduction.  A few weeks later this boy came by my house on a Saturday and asked if we could walk.  Of course, I was flattered, blushed a lot and we walked up and down the streets in my neighborhood, eventually holding hands while I blushed madly some more!  I thought that was the end of my pleasant walk and nothing more would come of it.  Oh, no!  My South River friend now was my avowed enemy because I had walked hand in hand with HER boyfriend and she challenged me to a fight.  I rolled my eyes and walked away.  That day at lunch I walked to one of the several hangouts we freshmen used for lunch.  As I approached the restaurant, out this angry girl flew into my face grabbing my hair screaming the whole very brief moment.  I managed to shove her away from me then turned and walked away.  I was very scared I would be attacked from behind, but I wasn’t!  Later, I heard my former, angry friend was calling out a girl in another clique.  My first thought was, “Oh, brother!  Here she goes again.”  This other girl was an excellent student from a wealthy family and had done nothing to deserve the fight she was challenged to.  I screwed up my courage and pride, walked into the coffee shop she and her friends went for lunch, and approached her.  She was quite surprised to see me.  I said to her I had heard she had been challenged to the fight.  I told her all she had to do is turn and walk away.  I said walking away would humiliate the angry girl and she had no answer for being walked away from.  Not long after that, I found out my family was moving again, this time to California.  On the last day of school we were given our year books and the opportunity to get them autographed.  The smart girl sought me out, thanked me for my advice - which worked - and wrote in my year book that I was nice, and wise, and wished we could have been friends the whole year.  She also told me she was sorry I was moving away.    I was reminded of these events by the discussion of hubs in creating greater chances of meeting  within the six degrees of possibility. When I moved to California I attended another particular high school - for one year.  Several years later, I moved to Portland, Oregon. I worked at an architectural firm.  One day, a woman I had never met ran up to my desk, put her hand over her heart and began to sing the school song of the of the high school I had attended my sophomore high school year!  The woman was the wife of one of the architects at the firm.  Several years after that I was working for a state senator, a very close friend of my husband and Godfather of my stepson.  The senator hired a woman to be the receptionist for his office.this woman was from Spotswood, New Jersey and attended South River High School one year ahead of me; though we never saw each other at South River or Spotswood, we knew people in common.  I have had many other similar connections while living in Oregon.  Six degrees of separations, indeed!

Author: @jpmoutinho
Content:
As someone who studied this field, this is a really great video. The reason I think this area is so interesting (why it blew up the way it did) is that it poses very simple models and most people can understand that still allow for complex emergent behaviour. I continue using this approach to most things I work on today.

Nitpick: in your preferential attachment simulation you made each appearing node connect to only 1 other node (with the right probability). This makes the network grow as a a tree (which you can observe in the animation). This does not fully represent the scale-free model. Instead, each new appearing node should potentially connect to ALL other nodes, each with the probability equal to 1/degree (with some normalization). This is a subtle differnece, but it will make a much better representation of what the model intends.
