Author: @adamsawyer1763
Content:
The issue of larger groups being less able to cooperate is not merely a function of the network connections. It's a result of individual'sinability to track and remember everyone's past moral decisions.

Humans are not homogenous. There are great differences in our tendencies to be pro-social and anti-social. I.e. to cooperate fairly or to exploit and cheat other people's fair cooperation.

Anthropology shows that in small groups humans detect and suppress sociopaths by either coercing them into prosocial behaviour or eliminating them by murder or exile.

However, in larger groups where some individuals are effectively hubs with vast numbers of connections AND exploitative life strategies these anti-sociopath cultural adaptations fail. In fact they are frequently exploited by the well connected sociopath and turned against the prosocial majority as part of a broader divide and rule strategy.

The problem is that intelligent sociopaths with a flair for networking can hide their immorality (many shallow social connections rather than fewer deep connections that foster real understanding of their true nature).

Also in a hierarchical society with lootable wealth there sociopaths can create incentive and reward structures that motivate others to abandon pro-social morality and support the sociopaths in their acquisition of power.

It's a complex system not explained by any one simple model. But these long-range network effects, especially hubs (super nodes) certainly contribute.

I would just strongly warn against the materialist view that the observed effects are all a matter of unconscious physical forces.

Humans are conscious agents who consciously make use of the natural environment and social structures to achieve their own ends. Just because you happen to be in the prosocial majority doesn't mean others aren't deliberately exploitative.

Author: @BokkiVA
Content:
When I was 10, I met another kid online through Skype. We’d both somehow ended up with the same random contact — not even a real friend, just a strange account — and started talking. It turned out we were into all the same games: GTA San Andreas Multiplayer, Urban Terror, Combat Arms, and a bunch of others.

Eventually, we started talking about school and realized we were both about to switch to a new one — the same one. We joked about trying to meet at the student gathering the next day, but since we didn’t know what each other looked like and neither of us wanted to share photos online, we figured we’d never spot each other in the crowd and gave up on the idea.

The next day, there was a small admission event where new students were being sorted into different classes. I started chatting with the kids around me, and the first person I spoke to — the one sitting on my right — turned out to be the same kid I’d met online the day before and we both got sorted into the same class under the same teacher.

It got even stranger. We also realized we had the same online friend, someone who was actually my best friend at the time, and he knew him really well too.

It still feels like a mystery how all of that lined up in just two days — especially since that school hadn’t even been my parents’ first choice, which makes the whole thing feel even more unlikely.

Author: @skyscraperfan
Content:
Marlon Brando probably is a bad example, as famous actors are hubs that are probably connected to most people by four or fewer steps. Take a famous actor like Brad Pitt today. He probably knows pretty much all other famous actors in Hollywood directly. If you take one step further, you already have that huge group of people who have ever worked with one of those famous actors. Another step further and the group will contain anyone who works of worked in the film and entertainment industry. So if you know one of those people, you are at most four, but likely only two or three steps from Brad Pitt. 

The same is true for politicians. You have probably met your local MP once or at least someone who knows him. That MP has very likely met your prime minister, chancellor, president or whatever the chief of government is called and that person has likely met Donald Trump. So you are at most four, but likely even less steps away from Donald Trump, if you like it or not.

That number of six may only be true for not very well connected people in different countries.

Author: @Napoleon_Bonapa
Content: I suppose this idea of connectivity is true, but I don't think it models things accurately. Because you have waves. You can't actually compute the importance of not-interconnection. As in radial information. For example, I can tell a joke to a friend on the street and a person passes by and finds that joke to be really funny. But he doesn't know me and I don't know him. If you plot the graph, who knows? We might be separated by at least 4 degrees, but information hops without being quantified by nods. And I don't think there's a way of doing a deterministic computation on this. Because you really fast hit the problem of complexity. Like when you try at billiards to put a ball in the pocket by hitting 8 or more sides of the table. You end up computing the spin of electrons for an accurate result. There are models that could in theory describe the propagation of information from a statistical perspective, but it can't be pin pointed to an individual's actions. As they say... Minority report? Impossible.

Content:
Back in 2004, My family and I visited Turkey. In a busy afternoon we were walking in a bazaar in Istanbul when we suddenly saw one of our cousins in front of us. He was a theater actor back then and as far as we knew, was touring Mexico to perform. This was one of the strangest "small world" moment I have ever encountered. Istanbul is a huge city, and Turkey was not our resident country. He was supposed to be on the other side of the world, yet we just saw him on the street like we were in a small town.
Now I know, it was the hub effect. Istanbul is a hub for travellers, and he was just between flights and wanted to check a bazaar in Istanbul when we meet.

Author: @a-guess-at-the-riddle
Content: Derek, how about an episode on science education (theory) vs confronting the unknown (anomaly/outliers and experiment). You see this distinction in things like unsupervised/supervised learning or clustering vs inference. But I find people don't understand the domain of the (speaking very roughly) 'pre-theoretic' because education focuses on the known and not the unknown (which is where scientists actually operate if on the cutting edge). A good concept here is 'scope' as outlier data that is outside our theories is characterized by vagueness. The theory (think 'semantic') scope is uncertain, something that can be elucidated in analogy to Linguistic's syntax vs semantics dichotomy. Coherent semantics implies valid syntax, but incoherent semantics doesn't imply invalid syntax ('Green ideas sleep furiously'). I wish people understood this aspect of inquiry more.

Author: @Waladil-v5l
Content:
I think that 100 people is a very low estimate of people we know in comparison to the breadth of acquaintances that were allowed in the first study. In that first example, we have: Friend, Co-worker, boyfriend, sorority sister, daughter, and producer on a movie (which is technically another form of co-worker but it illustrates a good point I'll get around to later). This represents a wide breadth of people both in terms of the social relationships but also temporally.

One I want to focus in on is the sorority sister relationship. Sorority sisters usually only know each other for up to four years. Presumably, they were not still sorority sisters at the time of the study, although that isn't clear. Sororities have something like 40-ish members, 25% of which rotate each year. So if you join as a freshman (freshwoman?) with a group of 10, there are 30 ahead of you and will be 30 behind you. So your reach within that sorority is 70 people. 

Don Juan DeMarco had over 200 people working on it, and presumably any one would have worked as the link to Marlon Brando. That film came out four years prior to the study (1995-1999) and in the intervening years Marlon Brando had been in three more movies: The Island of Dr. Moreau, The Brave, and Free Money. If each of those four total films had 200 people on the cast and crew, and we assume that 160 were a consistent "core cast" with only 40 new faces each time (which is a huge underestimation of the new people per movie, but roll with it), then we've got 320 people one step away from Marlon Brando on films he'd worked on in the last five years alone.  

What I'm illustrating here is that with a such a broad brush of "connections" that the number should probably be closer to 500 people, especially for anyone highly social. Every member of your family, every co-worker you've ever had, every person who was in a social group at the same time as you. I'm a relatively reclusive person, and I'd probably still be able to be used as a link to at least 300 people just from jobs and groups I was part of back in college.

Author: @jonadabtheunsightly
Content:
There's a significant amount of probably unavoidable selection bias in the empirical studies.  The people who would take the largest numbers of steps to connect to one another, inevitably don't get looked at because they're not connected to any of the researchers.  There are people out there in the world who would need multiple degrees of separation just to get beyond their own fairly insular people group.  There are people in the highlands of New Guinea who have never met anyone who speaks Tok Pisin or who has traveled more than a few hours' walk from their home.  Same thing in various Arctic-circle communities.  Same thing in the Kalahari.  Nobody ever calculates how many links those people need to connect to other people like that on the other side of the globe.  (And then there's that community in the Andaman Islands that has no connections to the outside world at all; but that's a special case.)

On the other hand, there are also organizations that bring together people who, as a group, _systematically_ interact with people in as many different places as possible.  If you look at anybody who attended Black Forest Academy, for example, they're going to know somebody who knows somebody from pretty much any country or ethnicity you care to name.  Which I guess makes it a "hub" in their model.

Author: @SenseiWarren
Content:
Once upon a time, we could access graphs and maps of all our friend connections on facebook, showing links between ourselves and our friend groups, and friends of friends, and so on. 
Now, those features are gone, and I can't find any 3rd party tools to accomplish similar tasks. 
Historical sites refer to "privacy concerns" as the reason this kind of feature disappeared... BUT the fact that network analysis is obviously being used, bought and sold by social media platforms strongly suggests that the real reason is that we are all easier to manipulate when that kind of information is a commercial commodity, rather than public information. 
We're not _allowed_ to see our network collectively precisely because having access to that perspective is too empowering, and therefore restricted to those who can pay for it.

This is my favorite kind of data science. The basic premise is so simple (6 degrees of Kevin Bacon) that it just almost seems instinctually obvious, but if you try to explain it, the "simple" concept becomes a far more complex series of systems that you didn't even think about. Author: @Felice_Enellen
Content:
I'm a long-time gamedev in the American tech hub of Seattle. Because of the large number of franchises I've worked on at muiltiple studios, my degree with almost anyone in the game industry, worldwide, is probably no more than 3, based on what I see on LinkedIn, even though I've been retired for ten years and new people keep joining. This is because they rapidly get to know people who either knew me or knew other people who knew me.

Also, because I've done movie license games that actually involved actors and crew from Hollywood, I'm like +1 step from similar people in the movie industry. As an aside, if I were an actor, rather than just a team member, and thus qualified for having one, my Bacon number would be 2.

Also, a lot of the gamedevs I've worked with went into other parts of the broader software/hardware/web industry, like Amazon, Nvidia, -Oculus- -Facebook- Meta, Cisco, etc., often ending up at high levels, so that most people in those companies would be one link away after meeting their managers or C-suite.

I also know people on a private, first-name basis in, or freshly-immigrated-from, nearly every US state, nearly every Canadian province, the UK, Australia, New Zealand, Japan, India, the Netherlands, Poland, Norway, Finland, Sweden, Germany, France, Lithuania, Turkey, Mexico, Honduras, Peru, Belize, and at this point I'm just kinda sick of listing places I know people. I think I got maybe 60-70% of them. I feel like I'm well-connected to every continent except maybe Africa. I sorta knew someone from South Africa once, but that's not much.

And so anyone who knows _me_ is automatically just 1 extra step from all of the the _local_ clusters in those places, even if they aren't otherwise very connected at all.

A lot of this is due to work and also my various personal travels. Some is due to making long-term good friends over the internet. The length of the list is probably pretty closely correlated to my ever-increasing age (sigh). But this is just how the world works now for most anyone who is online and personally mobile.

Author: @ramioren118
Content:
The video explores the social dynamics of interpersonal connections. The aspect that interested me most was the idea of hubs. This issue carries greater weight and significance in terms of social impact than individual relationships themselves.
People who are both highly connected and highly influential are, in effect, hubs for beliefs, opinions, and sociological or historical processes.
The specific question is: should one aspire to become a hub? And if so, how does one go about it?
A large number of famous people, for example, lack both influence and genuine connections, which means they are not true hubs of influence. Their success often rests on others who promote them. Likewise, wealthy individuals are not always hubs.
This is why, if I have a deep interest in an area—whether in art or science - it is crucial to connect with someone who is a hub in order to advance the idea. It is not always wise to try to become a hub oneself, as it can be a significant burden.
It is worthwhile, however, to have good, well-connected friends—as the saying goes, “With good friends, who needs favoritism?” Politicians are a clear example of hubs; so too are individuals of high social standing in the business, academic, or organizational world.
The problem that arises is that society as a whole becomes divided into hubs. On the one hand, this enables the rapid transfer of information between groups; on the other hand, it also breeds suspicion and hostility between groups. At the core of this issue lies the inner world (the psychology) of each group. By understanding the inner world of the person at the center of a hub, we can appreciate both the advantages of their central role and the dangers that surround them.
This field is fascinating—and I offer heartfelt thanks to Derek Muller, who presented the topic so beautifully. Your videos are a model of excellence in education and in the transmission of knowledge and values.

Author: @Gab-xr1os
Content: Great video, as always! I just want to point out that the situation presented at 1:54 is flawed, not only because it supposes that each connection is totally random, but also because it assumes that the population is infinite! Otherwise, the probability of some of those people knowing the same people isn't 0 and grows very quickly with each step. Also, even with the infinite population supposition, you'd have to subtract yourself! If I know 100 persons that each know 100 persons, they all know me! So even if the population is infinite, that's 100^2-99 = 9 901 people that I know at 2 steps, not  100^2 = 10 000. I know it doesn't change the conclusion, but what I like about your videos is when you manage to explain clearly some complicated concepts — without saying anything false!

Author: @ResistanceIsUsefull
Content:
Stanley Milgram, a social psychologist, is credited with originating the concept of six degrees of separation through his "small-world experiment" conducted in the 1960s.

 In this experiment, Milgram sent letters to 160 individuals in Nebraska, instructing them to forward the letter to a stockbroker in Boston using only personal acquaintances. The goal was to determine the average number of intermediaries required to connect two random individuals. The results showed that the letters that successfully reached their destination did so in an average of five to six steps, with a median of five intermediaries.  This finding led to the popular idea that any two people in the world are connected by no more than six degrees of separation.

Milgram's work was inspired by earlier ideas, including a 1929 essay by Hungarian writer Frigyes Karinthy, who proposed that any two people could be connected through a chain of five intermediaries.  Milgram's experiment provided the first empirical test of this concept, although he did not use the phrase "six degrees of separation" himself.

The idea gained widespread popularity after being featured in the 1990 play and 1993 film Six Degrees of Separation, which popularized the phrase.

Despite the widespread acceptance of the theory, the original experiment had limitations. Only a small percentage of the letters actually reached their destination, with some studies reporting a completion rate of around 30%.
 The high attrition rate was attributed to participants not following through with the chain.

 Furthermore, the experiment was based on a single target person in a specific location, which may not be representative of global connectivity.
 More recent studies using digital networks, such as Facebook and email, have found similar average path lengths of five to six steps, supporting Milgram's core finding.

Milgram's work also introduced the concept of "Connectors"—individuals who are highly connected and play a crucial role in linking different social groups.  However, more recent research by Duncan Watts suggests that these hubs may not be as influential in spreading information as previously thought, with only a small percentage of messages passing through them.

The phenomenon has since become a foundational concept in network theory, influencing fields such as sociology, computer science, and epidemiology.

Author: @Tyler-s2e
Content:
Quick headline summary

Gun violence (U.S.): a large, population-level public-health crisis — tens of thousands of deaths per year. Firearm deaths climbed sharply around 2020–2021 (pandemic era); suicides make up the majority of firearm deaths and reached record levels in recent years, while homicides spiked in 2020–2021 and remained near historically high levels through 2023. 

Substance use in medical professionals: an occupational/clinical problem concentrated within a workforce population. Prevalence estimates vary by profession and measure (hazardous alcohol use meta-estimates ~10–15%; some nursing estimates cite 14–20% for problematic use; prescription misuse among clinicians is also reported but figures vary by study). The problem is persistent and linked to burnout, stress, access to controlled substances, and stigma that delays help-seeking. 

Scale & trend (numbers matter)

Gun violence

~46,700 total firearm deaths in 2023 (including ~27,300 firearm suicides and ~17,927 homicides). Firearm suicides represented a majority of firearm deaths in 2023. Recent years (2020–2023) show higher overall firearm mortality than much of the prior decade, with a pandemic-era surge and then modest declines in some measures but overall levels remaining high. 

Substance use among health professionals

Estimates depend on measure & group: a meta-analysis and reviews place hazardous alcohol use in health professionals around ~13%; some nursing-specific figures (from nursing organizations and treatment resources) put dependence/problem use estimates in the mid-teens (14–20%) range; physician prescription-drug misuse estimates are heterogeneous (some surveys report high lifetime experimentation, but confirmed current-disorder prevalence is lower). These are workforce-level percentages, not population deaths. 

Different kinds of harms (why they’re not directly comparable)

Gun violence is a population-level cause of death and injury — immediate, often lethal (tens of thousands dead yearly, many more injured), with broad community ripple effects. It’s concentrated across demographics (higher homicide rates among certain groups and ages; suicides concentrated in adults) and geographic hotspots. 

Substance misuse in clinicians is an occupational health and patient-safety issue — it affects clinicians’ health, career, and can raise risks to patients (errors, impaired judgment), but the number of clinician deaths from substance use is far smaller in absolute terms than firearm deaths in the general population. Its importance lies in workforce capacity, patient safety, and stigma/rehabilitation systems. 

Shared drivers and intersections

Stress, trauma, and the pandemic: Both trends were influenced by the COVID-19 era. The pandemic corresponded with spikes in community violence (including firearm homicides) and also increased stress, burnout, and mental-health strain among clinicians, which is associated with higher substance misuse risk. 

Workplace violence & clinician mental health: Hospitals report rising workplace violence; violence against staff contributes to trauma, absenteeism, turnover, and can increase risk of burnout/substance use among workers. The AHA documents large downstream costs and mental-health effects for health systems. 

Health-system impacts

Gun violence: Increases emergency caseloads, trauma system strain, cost of care, long-term disability burden, and public-health resource needs (prevention, community programs). 
Bloomberg School of Public Health

Substance use in clinicians: Raises concerns about impaired practice, increases use of clinician-health programs, monitoring/licensure issues, staff shortages (suspensions, leave), and costs for treatment/reintegration. It also affects morale and retention. 

Typical policy & intervention responses

For gun violence

Population-level prevention: background checks, safe-storage laws, extreme risk protection orders, community violence interruption programs, investment in mental-health and crisis services, targeted community interventions in high-violence neighborhoods. Evidence and politics vary by strategy and place. 

For substance use among clinicians

Occupational interventions: confidential physician/clinician health programs (treatment + monitoring), employee assistance programs, workplace culture change to reduce stigma, improved access to mental-health care, diversion control for controlled substances, fatigue/burnout mitigation (scheduling, staffing), and re-entry programs for treated clinicians. These reduce harm and preserve workforce capacity. 

Key takeaways (short)

Magnitude: Gun violence causes tens of thousands of deaths per year in the U.S. (a major population-level mortality driver). Substance misuse among health professionals affects a significant minority of the workforce (estimates vary ~10–20% for hazardous use in some groups) and primarily raises occupational and patient-safety concerns rather than producing comparable mortality totals. 

Trends: Both problems worsened in the pandemic era (2020–2021) — firearm deaths surged and have stayed at historically high levels; clinician substance-use risk increased alongside burnout and workplace stress. 

Intersections: Violence in healthcare settings contributes to clinician trauma and burnout, which can increase vulnerability to substance misuse — so preventing workplace violence is a point of overlap.

Content:
“The ShotSpotter Problem”

At Pennedale University, students argued passionately about gun control laws. They demanded stricter regulations, background checks, bans, and registries. Everyone agreed that someone else should be disarmed — not their roommates, cousins, or that guy down the hall with an unlicensed Glock.

The rule was simple: if you knew about an illegal gun, you didn’t tell the police. You told Antifa, who promised to use it “responsibly.” Reporting it to the authorities would only empower the system, which was, according to Antifa, fascist. Besides, the police already knew. They just pretended not to know. That way, when a student finally got caught, everyone could be shocked.

Meanwhile, private security had installed “environmental monitoring devices” around campus. These were officially for detecting loud noises and ensuring community safety. Everyone knew they were ShotSpotters. And everyone knew the CIA hacked ShotSpotters. And everyone knew the CIA didn’t hack ShotSpotters. The certainty of both positions at once was what made it credible.

The program was called MKTrans. It was designed to identify vulnerable children for mind control. Nobody knew what MKTrans stood for, but everyone agreed it stood for something important. The CIA used it to recruit spies. Not real spies, of course — unwitting idiots. The theory was that idiots made the best spies because they never knew they were spying. If someone asked whether they were spying, they could honestly say no. That made them more credible than spies who actually knew what they were doing.

Lena, a psychology major, tried to get clarification from the dean. The dean explained that ShotSpotters did not exist, but if they did exist, they could not possibly be hacked, and if they were hacked, it was only to protect students from terrorism, which did not exist, except when it did.

“Then what about MKTrans?” she asked.

“MKTrans is not real,” the dean said. “And if it were real, it would be classified. And if it weren’t classified, it would be perfectly harmless. And if it were harmful, it would be in the best interests of national security. Do you see the problem?”

“Yes,” Lena said.

“Good. Then don’t talk about it.”

By the end of the semester, the protests about gun control grew so loud that no one could hear the ShotSpotters going off at night. Or maybe they weren’t going off. Or maybe they were recording the protests. Nobody knew. Nobody cared. Everyone was certain something was happening — and they were equally certain that nothing was happening at all.

And that was how Pennedale University kept its students safe: by ensuring they were too confused to notice whether they were in danger.

network science the number 6

When I close my eyes while facing the sun, I consistently perceive a dotted figure shaped like the number six. At first, this might seem like a simple byproduct of light stimulating the retina, creating random visual noise known as phosphenes. However, the persistence and specificity of the “6” form invite deeper reflection. Our brains are wired to impose familiar patterns onto ambiguity — a phenomenon known as pareidolia — and the number six is more than a numeral; it is a powerful symbol of interconnectedness in both culture and mathematics. 

The theory of six degrees of separation suggests that all people are linked by no more than six social steps, an idea further accelerated by the rise of the internet and global communication. The “6” I see becomes more than a visual artifact; it feels like a neurological echo of a deeper truth — that human perception and cognition are naturally attuned to recognize connection, not just in the world around us, but even in the shadows behind our closed eyes.

The number 6 already carries huge cultural and mathematical significance:
Six degrees of separation: everyone is connected on average by ~6 steps.
Hexagons/6-sided shapes: nature’s efficiency (beehives, snowflakes).
The internet & connection: with modern networks, the idea of “6” as the number of universal connection is embedded in our culture.

Content: The one thing I don't want is crazy people changing the world.

In a related but different thought, I've considered my typical trip to a store in my city. Walmart, Target, Kroger, Publix, etc. I go in, and I never recognize people, except for employees. And so I've thought (in the shower of course), in any instance I'm in one of these stores, what is the probability that I'm in the store AGAIN with a shopper who I had been in the store with previously? Or even better, how many times per year can I expect to be in a store with the same person? How about the same person but different stores? It's probably an impossible calculation due to all the variables involved, but something tells me, like the six-degrees-of-separation problem, it's more common than we'd anticipate.

Author: @RandomWombleP
Content: One thing that the simple 2 option simulations, where 1 is deemed to be be negative (defecting) and one is deemed to be positive (cooperating) does not account for is different point of view, it assumes the same outcome is equally good for everyone. The video seems to end on a slightly more positive note on the basis that if people can choose who they associate with then in the end then the positive choice (cooperating) becomes the default. However a more realistic representation of the way the world currently works would be for some players/nodes to have defecting as the more positive result and cooperating as the negative one. In that situation if players/nodes can choose who they associate with instead of 1 result winning over the other I suspect you would end up with 2 separate clusters, one which always defects and one which always cooperates which is the way the world is going, particularly online, with very polarised groups.

Content: There was a Norwegian TV program that put this theory to the test. It ran for 12 episodes, meaning 12 different experiments were carried out. In each episode, a pair of hosts were dropped in completely random places around the world, for example, deep in the jungle, on the Tibetan tundra, or in a small African village. Their mission was to reach a specific celebrity, often a Hollywood actor. Starting from where they were left, they had to rely solely on talking to locals and building connections until they eventually reached the celebrity. In all but one of the episodes, they actually succeeded. So yes, the theory holds true.

My takeaway here is that if people communicate, they then to realise that cooperation wins because we gain more as a group if we work together. 6 is greater than 5. This is the same game played at the group level. Emergent layering of tribes into teams).

This explains so much about why we have such and such myths or stories about morality and codes of conduct. 

Working together always, no matter what, is the message of many religions, and the true best answer here too. If you take the premise that we share the world. The boundaries for the ultimate group is the planet. We are all in the same jar. But if we all share, we all win, and the results are maximized. We get the whole 6 points total every round.
